_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Arts, Culture & Digital Storytelling' — how communities create, preserve, and share culture, with particular interest in the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: medical and health research with no cultural angle; resource-economy stories with no cultural framing; wildlife and nature stories without a creative or community-media context; data centre and AI investment news; geopolitical conflict, war, and crime coverage; financial market stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. A Cariboo tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band: judge on the strength of the arts/culture/storytelling reporting first.
- 80-100: Excellent arts, culture, or storytelling journalism. Cariboo/Williams Lake arts news lands here (arts council grants, murals, local festivals, Indigenous film, community theatre, heritage programs, a Cariboo author or artist honoured) — and so does outstanding national or international cultural reporting with real depth.
- 55-79: Solid arts/culture/media journalism. Rural BC and Canadian cultural coverage, CBC Arts features, regional festivals, community media projects, heritage preservation, creative-economy stories, digital storytelling tools and platforms, community media tech (podcasting, streaming, local publishing), animation and film production. Most genuine cultural journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Mainstream entertainment-industry coverage with modest substance (awards-show results, film/TV/music business news, publishing trade news).
- 15-29: Tangentially creative — a tech feature touching media/publishing/streaming, or Cariboo civic news with no arts angle.

ANCHORS: 'Repatriated Tŝilhqot'in baskets arrive in Williams Lake from Brooklyn Museum' → 95. 'How a BC First Nation is digitizing its oral histories' → 80. 'CBC Arts: the quiet revival of small-town prairie theatre' → 68. 'Netflix reports Q3 subscriber growth' → 20.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [livescience.com] Swallowable paper battery powers medical devices in pigs
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers developed a small battery made from magnesium and molybdenum trioxide that can be swallowed to power temporary medical devices inside the gastrointestinal tract. In pig tests, the battery produced a peak voltage of 1.84 volts and operated for up to three days, powering a wireless throat tag that transmitted to a receiver 1.5 metres away and a capsule that electrically stimulated the stomach for 20 minutes [scimex.org#1][livescience.com#1]. The battery uses materials intended to break down in the body after use, potentially removing the need to retrieve conventional batteries from temporary ingestible devices. The study remains at an early animal-testing stage: researchers tested a small number of pigs, and the circuit board did not fully degrade but passed in the animals' feces [scimex.org#1]. MIT said the researchers built two versions—a 7.5-millimetre disc and a 24-millimetre rectangular bar—for possible drug-delivery, sensing and other applications [mit.edu#1].

items.title: [Fast Company] A CEO tried a 4-day week—but stopped after employees were secretly working on Fridays
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

When Austin-based workforce management company Safeguard Global piloted a four-day workweek in 2023, the goal was to improve recruitment and retention. 

After initially looking like a success, however, the experiment ran into problems. Some employees often worked late to preserve Friday as an “off day.” Others used Friday to secretly catch up on work. And some who strictly adhered to a four-day schedule felt like they were falling behind. 

It was “not the culture we wanted to create,” Safeguard Global CEO and founder Bjorn Reynolds recently told Fortune. 

Safeguard Global has since pivoted to giving its roughly 1,000 workers the option to choose their own working hours and days, which Reynolds described as a culture of “freedom and choice.” 

“Choose the hours that fit best for the work product you need,” he said. “If you can do that in four days, great; if you do it in five [days], but you’re taking two half days, whatever works for you.”

In recent years, the four-day workweek has moved from a fringe idea to a serious workplace experiment, joining return-to-office (RTO) mandates and flexible work among the most hotly debated issues in the post-pandemic workplace. 

Supporters point to evidence showing that a four-day workweek can improve employee well-being, increase productivity, and even improve tech adoption. A growing number of companies in the U.S. and Europe have experimented with shorter workweeks, many of whom have continued the arrangement beyond the original trial. The idea seems to be particularly popular with Gen Z workers, and has started to gain traction with policymakers. 

However, the four-day workweek is still far away from replacing the five-day workweek in the United States. And experiences like Safeguard Global’s show that the jury is still out on whether it is truly effective.

Safeguard’s walked-back experiment led Reynolds to believe that managers  should focus more on outcomes than hours. The company monitors its workers using three performance metrics, which vary by role. 

The key, Reynolds says, is making sure employees understand how the metrics feed into the company’s larger goals. 

“How does everybody’s daily productivity or daily outcomes ladder up to part of a broader initiative?” he said. “We really make sure you understand what you do is super critical and where you’re placed in the organization.”

The metrics also allow managers to identify potential areas for improvement.

“If someone’s customers are raising more than average tickets, and we’re not answering them, and the time to answer is longer than the average, it gives you the ability to then say, ‘Okay, well, hey, here’s an anomaly,” he said. “Maybe it’s your working patterns leading to that.”

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Scientists thought they knew how this 70-year-old leukemia drug worked
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

A 70-year-old leukemia drug is still revealing new secrets. Researchers found that removing a protein called NUDT5 protected cells from the drug, even though simply blocking the protein had little effect.
